---
title: "Indicator species"
description: "Indicator species analysis (indicspecies multipatt) and differential abundance with mvabund for microbiome OTUs in R."
format: html
editor: visual
---

[Beta diversity](beta-div.qmd) showed that the fungal communities differ between land uses. Which OTUs are responsible for these differences? Several methods can identify OTUs associated with a group of samples. This section documents two of them:

-   **Indicator species analysis** (indicspecies package), a permutation test of the association of each OTU with one group or a combination of groups;
-   **Regression models for multivariate abundances** (mvabund package), which fit a generalised linear model (GLM) to each OTU.

To follow the example presented on this page directly on your computer, download the script `030_diff_abund.R` and the example data by clicking the buttons below. Alternatively, you may copy the codes below into your own script, and use your own data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
library(downloadthis)
library(phyloseq)
library(indicspecies)
library(mvabund)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
load("../../RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
```

```{r}
#| layout: [[-10,35,-5,40,-10]]
#| echo: false
download_file(
  path = "../../scripts/ITS/030_diff_abund.R",
  output_name = "030_diff_abund",
  button_label = "Download script",
  button_type = "success",
  has_icon = TRUE,
  icon = "fa fa-save",
  self_contained = FALSE
)

download_file(
  path = "../../RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData",
  output_name = "ITS_otu_BLAST_clean",
  button_label = "Download example RData",
  button_type = "success",
  has_icon = TRUE,
  icon = "fa fa-save",
  self_contained = FALSE
)
```

To get started, load the OTU table filtered with BLAST (see [BLAST filtering](../otu-tables/filter/BLAST.qmd)), and set the seed for the rarefaction and the permutation tests. We also order the land uses from agriculture to the old forest, and define their colours for the plots.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Load the cleaned OTU table from previous scripts
load("RData/ITS/otu_BLAST_clean.RData")
```

```{r}
set.seed(100)

sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$Land_use <- factor(
  sample_data(otu_BLAST_clean)$Land_use,
  levels = c("Conventional agriculture", "Organic agriculture", "Grassland",
             "Oak", "Old Ref"))

land_use_col <- c("Conventional agriculture" = "bisque",
                  "Organic agriculture" = "bisque3",
                  "Grassland" = "orange",
                  "Oak" = "darkolivegreen2",
                  "Old Ref" = "turquoise4")
```

## Data preparation

As in [Alpha diversity](alpha-div.qmd#rarefaction) and [Beta diversity](beta-div.qmd), we start from the data rarefied to 1011 reads (same seed, so the same rarefied table).

```{r}
#| message: false
otu_table_rarefy <- rarefy_even_depth(otu_BLAST_clean, sample.size = 1011,
                                      replace = FALSE, rngseed = 100,
                                      verbose = FALSE)
nsamples(otu_table_rarefy)
ntaxa(otu_table_rarefy)
```

indicspecies and mvabund do not work with phyloseq objects: they need the OTU table as a matrix with the samples as rows and the OTUs as columns. In our phyloseq object the OTUs are the rows (`taxa_are_rows = TRUE`), so the table is transposed. We also extract the metadata and the taxonomy.

```{r}
taxa_are_rows(otu_table_rarefy)
otu_mat <- t(as(otu_table(otu_table_rarefy), "matrix"))
dim(otu_mat)

meta_rare <- data.frame(sample_data(otu_table_rarefy))
tax_rare  <- data.frame(tax_table(otu_table_rarefy))[, c("phylum", "class",
                                                         "order", "family",
                                                         "genus", "species")]

# Check that the samples are in the same order in the matrix and the metadata
all(rownames(otu_mat) == rownames(meta_rare))

table(meta_rare$Land_use)
```

The groups are unbalanced: 51 samples in the oak plantations (6 sites), 9 in each of the other land uses (1 site each).

## Indicator species analysis

Indicator species analysis [@decaceres2009] tests, for each OTU, how strongly it is associated with a group of samples (here, a land use). `indicspecies::multipatt()` also tests combinations of groups: an OTU can be associated with several land uses together (e.g. both agricultural land uses), not only with one [@decaceres2010].

Two association indices are commonly used:

-   **IndVal** (`"IndVal.g"`): combines the specificity of the OTU (is it found mostly in this group?) and its fidelity (is it found in most samples of this group?). It only looks for OTUs that are associated with a group (preference).
-   **Point-biserial correlation** (`"r.g"`): the correlation between the abundance of the OTU and the membership to a group. It can also be negative (avoidance), and it considers the abundances outside the group.

As in the tutorial, we use `"r.g"`. The `.g` versions correct for the different number of samples in each group, important here because the oak group has many more samples. The p-values are obtained by permutations: the samples are randomly assigned to the groups 999 times. This takes about 30 seconds.

```{r}
set.seed(100)
indval <- multipatt(otu_mat, meta_rare$Land_use, func = "r.g",
                    control = how(nperm = 999))
```

The results are in `indval$sign`: for each OTU, the columns `s.<group>` show to which group(s) it is associated (1 = yes), `index` the number of the group combination, `stat` the value of the correlation and `p.value` the p-value of the permutation test.

```{r}
head(indval$sign)
```

`summary()` lists the OTUs with a p-value lower than `alpha`, grouped by land use combination. The list is long (one line per OTU); only the first lines are shown here.

```{r}
#| eval: false
summary(indval, alpha = 0.001)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
cat(head(capture.output(summary(indval, alpha = 0.001)), 20), sep = "\n")
cat("...\n")
```

### Multiple testing

One test is done for each of the 5153 OTUs. With a threshold of 0.05, about 5% of the OTUs (\~250) would be significant by chance only. The tutorial therefore uses a stricter threshold of p ≤ 0.001.

```{r}
sum(indval$sign$p.value <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(indval$sign$p.value <= 0.001, na.rm = TRUE)
```

The p-values can also be corrected for multiple testing, e.g. with the false discovery rate (FDR) of Benjamini & Hochberg. With 999 permutations, the smallest possible p-value is 0.001: to obtain smaller corrected p-values, more permutations would be needed.

```{r}
p_fdr <- p.adjust(indval$sign$p.value, method = "fdr")
sum(p_fdr <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

We keep the OTUs with p ≤ 0.001, as in the tutorial: 280 OTUs (tutorial: 287).

```{r}
indval_sig <- subset(indval$sign, p.value <= 0.001)
nrow(indval_sig)
```

### Table of the indicator OTUs

We add the name of the land use(s) each OTU is associated with (the columns of `indval$comb` are all the combinations of land uses, in the order of `index`) and the taxonomy, and sort the table by land use combination and by strength of the association.

```{r}
indval_sig$Land_uses <- colnames(indval$comb)[indval_sig$index]

indval_tab <- cbind(indval_sig[, c("Land_uses", "stat", "p.value")],
                    tax_rare[rownames(indval_sig), ])
indval_tab <- indval_tab[order(indval_sig$index, -indval_sig$stat), ]
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
head(indval_tab, 20)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(head(indval_tab, 20), digits = 3)
```

```{r}
sort(table(indval_tab$Land_uses), decreasing = TRUE)
```

Most indicator OTUs are associated with a single land use: grassland (74), organic agriculture (59), conventional agriculture (57) and the old forest (55). Only 2 OTUs are indicators of the oak plantations alone. The six plantations differ from each other (see [Beta diversity](beta-div.qmd)), so few OTUs are found consistently in all of them. 20 OTUs are associated with both agricultural land uses together.

### Taxonomy of the indicator OTUs

We count the indicator OTUs per land use (or combination) and phylum. The OTUs without a phylum are "Unidentified", and the phyla with few indicator OTUs are grouped as "Other" (the colour palette has 8 colours).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
indval_tab$phylum_plot <- ifelse(is.na(indval_tab$phylum) |
                                   indval_tab$phylum == "NA",
                                 "Unidentified", indval_tab$phylum)
top_phyla <- names(sort(table(indval_tab$phylum_plot), decreasing = TRUE))[1:7]
indval_tab$phylum_plot[!indval_tab$phylum_plot %in% top_phyla] <- "Other"

indval_phylum <- count(indval_tab, Land_uses, phylum = phylum_plot)

# Order the land use combinations by their index (single land uses at the
# top of the plot), and put "Other" and "Unidentified" at the end of the
# legend
indval_phylum$Land_uses <- factor(
  indval_phylum$Land_uses,
  levels = rev(unique(indval_tab$Land_uses)))
indval_phylum$phylum <- factor(
  indval_phylum$phylum,
  levels = c(sort(setdiff(top_phyla, c("Other", "Unidentified"))),
             "Other", "Unidentified"))

p_indval_phylum <- ggplot(indval_phylum,
                          aes(x = n, y = Land_uses, fill = phylum)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(x = "Number of indicator OTUs", y = NULL, fill = "Phylum") +
  theme_bw()
p_indval_phylum
```

Ascomycota are the most common indicators of the agricultural land uses and the grassland. Many indicators of the old forest belong to Rozellomycota (20 of 55 OTUs), a group of parasites of other fungi and protists, mostly known from environmental sequences.

### Plot of selected indicator OTUs

We plot the abundance of the strongest indicator OTU of each single land use. The OTU names are long sequence identifiers, so the plot labels use the genus (or the lowest identified rank) instead. `psmelt()` converts the phyloseq object into a long data frame (one row per OTU and sample), convenient for ggplot.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
top_otus <- indval_tab %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("OTU") %>%
  filter(Land_uses %in% levels(meta_rare$Land_use)) %>%
  group_by(Land_uses) %>%
  slice_max(stat, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(factor(Land_uses, levels = levels(meta_rare$Land_use)))
top_otus[, c("OTU", "Land_uses", "stat", "phylum", "genus")]

top_df <- psmelt(prune_taxa(top_otus$OTU, otu_table_rarefy))

# Label of each OTU: land use it indicates, and lowest identified rank
top_otus$label <- paste0(
  top_otus$Land_uses, "\n",
  apply(top_otus[, c("phylum", "class", "order", "family", "genus")], 1,
        function(x) tail(x[!is.na(x) & x != "NA"], 1)))
top_df$label <- factor(top_otus$label[match(top_df$OTU, top_otus$OTU)],
                       levels = top_otus$label)

p_indval_otus <- ggplot(top_df, aes(x = Land_use, y = Abundance)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(aes(colour = Land_use), size = 2, width = 0.2, height = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = land_use_col) +
  facet_wrap(~ label, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of reads (rarefied)", colour = "Land use") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
p_indval_otus
```

The strongest indicators of the agricultural land uses and of the grassland are abundant in all samples of their land use and rare or absent elsewhere, e.g. the *Mortierella* OTU of organic agriculture (r = 0.97) has 7 to 18 reads in every organic agriculture sample, and almost none in the other land uses. The indicator of the oak plantations, a *Penicillium* OTU, has a weaker association (r = 0.65): it is absent from the open land uses, but its abundance varies a lot between the plantation samples, and it is also found in the old forest. The indicator of the old forest, a *Solicoccozyma* OTU, is present in all land uses but much more abundant in the old forest: the point-biserial correlation also detects differences in abundance, not only in presence.

::: callout-note
Indicator OTUs are useful to describe the groups, but the taxonomy of many of them is incomplete: e.g. the indicator of conventional agriculture is only identified to the family Plectosphaerellaceae.
:::

## Regression models for multivariate abundances

Indicator species analysis uses permutation tests, which do not account for the strong mean-variance relationship of count data: abundant OTUs also vary much more between samples (overdispersion). An alternative is to fit a generalised linear model (GLM) to each OTU, with a distribution suited to overdispersed counts, such as the negative binomial. The mvabund package [@wang2012] fits these models with `manyglm()` and tests them with resampling (bootstrap).

Resampling is slow with many OTUs. To keep the computation time short, we only use the OTUs present in at least 10% of the samples (9 of 87): rare OTUs, present in a few samples, carry little information for a GLM anyway.

```{r}
prev <- colSums(otu_mat > 0)
otu_mat_prev <- otu_mat[, prev >= 9]
ncol(otu_mat_prev)
```

We convert the matrix into an mvabund object, and fit a negative binomial GLM to each OTU, with the land use as explanatory variable.

```{r}
otu_mvabund <- mvabund(otu_mat_prev)

glm_lu <- manyglm(otu_mvabund ~ Land_use, data = meta_rare,
                  family = "negative.binomial")
```

Check the model: the residuals should be spread randomly around 0, without a fan shape (which would mean that the negative binomial distribution does not describe the mean-variance relationship well).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
plot(glm_lu)
```

The residuals are spread evenly around 0, without a fan shape: the negative binomial distribution is suitable. The vertical lines on the left are OTUs that are absent from all samples of a land use (very low predicted abundance); they are common with sparse data such as OTU tables.

We test the effect of the land use with `anova()`. `nBoot` is the number of bootstrap resamplings: we use 100 for a fast (about 1 minute) but less precise result. For a publication, use e.g. 999. `p.uni = "adjusted"` also tests each OTU separately, with p-values adjusted for multiple testing.

```{r}
set.seed(100)
anova_lu <- anova(glm_lu, nBoot = 100, p.uni = "adjusted",
                  show.time = "none")
```

```{r}
# Multivariate test: does the land use affect the community as a whole?
anova_lu$table
```

mvabund changes the OTU names that start with a number (it adds an "X"), so we take the names from our matrix instead (same order).

```{r}
# Univariate tests: which OTUs differ between land uses?
p_uni <- anova_lu$uni.p["Land_use", ]
otus_glm_sig <- colnames(otu_mat_prev)[p_uni <= 0.05]
length(otus_glm_sig)
```

The land use has a significant effect on the community as a whole (p = 0.01, the smallest p-value possible with 100 resamplings: 1/101). 180 of the 402 OTUs differ significantly between land uses (adjusted p ≤ 0.05).

### Coefficients

The coefficients of the significant OTUs (one column per OTU). The reference (intercept) is the first level of `Land_use`, conventional agriculture. A negative coefficient means that the OTU is less abundant in that land use than in conventional agriculture, a positive one that it is more abundant. We look at the 6 most abundant significant OTUs.

```{r}
coefs <- coef(glm_lu)[, p_uni <= 0.05]
colnames(coefs) <- otus_glm_sig

top_glm <- names(sort(colSums(otu_mat_prev[, otus_glm_sig]),
                      decreasing = TRUE))[1:6]
tax_rare[top_glm, c("phylum", "order", "genus")]
round(coefs[, top_glm], 2)
```

How to interpret the coefficients? `manyglm` uses a negative binomial distribution with a log link: the coefficients are on a natural log scale. To obtain the fold change, take the exponential of the coefficient. For example, a coefficient of -1.38 gives $e^{-1.38} = 0.25$: the OTU is 4 times less abundant (75% reduction) than in the reference land use. Very large coefficients (e.g. -15 or less, +15 or more) mean that the OTU is absent from a land use: the log of 0 is minus infinity, and the model returns a very large number instead.

```{r}
round(exp(coefs[, top_glm]), 2)
```

Examples:

-   The Plectosphaerellaceae OTU (the strongest indicator of conventional agriculture) has on average $e^{5.36} = 213$ reads in conventional agriculture. It is 0.39 times as abundant in organic agriculture (61% less), and 0.01 to 0.03 times as abundant in the other land uses.
-   The *Solicoccozyma* OTU (indicator of the old forest) is 6.45 times more abundant in the old forest than in conventional agriculture.
-   The three *Cortinarius* OTUs (ectomycorrhizal fungi) are absent from the agricultural land uses and the grassland: the intercept is -14.82 and the coefficients of the forests are very large (+15 to +19). They depend on the oak trees. One of them is found only in the plantations.

### Comparison with the indicator species analysis

How many of the OTUs selected by `manyglm` are also indicators (p ≤ 0.001)? Only the prevalent OTUs were tested with `manyglm`, so we compare within these 402 OTUs.

```{r}
indval_prev <- intersect(rownames(indval_sig), colnames(otu_mat_prev))
length(indval_prev)                          # indicators among the 402 OTUs
length(intersect(indval_prev, otus_glm_sig)) # selected by both methods
```

Among the 402 prevalent OTUs, 143 are indicators, and 118 of them are also selected by `manyglm`. `manyglm` selects 62 more OTUs: it tests any difference in abundance between land uses, while the indicator species analysis looks for OTUs associated with a specific group (or combination of groups). The two methods largely agree on the OTUs that differ most strongly between land uses.

::: callout-tip
## DESeq2

Another popular method is DESeq2 [@love2014], which also fits negative binomial GLMs, on the raw (non-rarefied) counts, with its own normalisation. phyloseq objects can be converted with `phyloseq::phyloseq_to_deseq2()`. DESeq2 (Bioconductor) is not installed by `001_required_packages.R`.
:::

## Exercise

Which OTUs are associated with the age of the oak plantations?

Hints:

-   Keep only the samples of the land use "Oak" with `subset_samples()` on `otu_table_rarefy`, and remove the OTUs that are no longer present with `prune_taxa(taxa_sums(x) > 0, x)`.
-   Run `multipatt()` with the site (`SiteID`) as the groups. Which plantations share indicator OTUs?
-   Look at the taxonomy of the indicators of the youngest (Oak_20) and the oldest (Oak_54) plantations. Do you find ectomycorrhizal genera (e.g. *Cortinarius*, *Russula*, *Tomentella*)?
